newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Council gives green light to Albania force.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Council gives green light to Albania force.

text.p: The U.N. Security Council late on Friday authorised an Italian-led force to guard deliveries of food in Albania and other necessities and help the country recover from violence and near-anarchy.

The vote was 14 to 0 with China abstaining on a resolution that invoked Chapter 7 of the U.N. Charter, which permits the use of force. In this case, the resolution said force could be used in self-defence.

China's representative told the council that Beijing disapproved of resolution that allowed the use of force and that the crisis in Albania was an internal affair. But Quin Huasun said he did not use his veto to stop the operation because of the request for help from the Albanian government.

The mandate of the force -- approved by, but not under U.N. auspices -- runs for three months at which time the council can decide whether it should be extended. The operation will be financed by participating nations.
Among those expressing willingness to send troops are France, Portugal, Spain, Greece, Turkey, Romania and Austria in addition to Italy.
The council also welcomed an offer by Italy, contained in a separate letter, to take the lead in organising and commanding the "multinational protection force."

Its purpose, the resolution said, was to "facilitate the safe and prompt delivery of humanitarian assistance and to help create a secure environment for the missions of international organisations in Albania."

Albania was swept by violence in January when a string of popular savings schemes collapsed, erasing millions of dollars. Rebels seized the south in March in an armed insurrection, blaming President Sali Berisha for the fiasco and demanding that he quit.
Since then gangs have roamed the south, stealing, looting, killing and creating a food crisis, prompting the government to ask for foreign military assistance.
The resolution also stressed that the crisis in Albania was a threat to peace in the region, a veiled reference to fears of another Balkan war if unrest spills over the border.

Hostilities have flared frequently in Serbia's Kosovo province to the north where 1.2 million Albanians live. To the east Albanians constitute about a quarter of the population in the former Yugoslav republic of Macedonia where U.S. troops lead a United Nations peacekeeping operation.

Italy's ambassador Paolo Fulci told reporters he was gratified the council moved "at astronomical speed." He said any operation had risks "but if you feed the people they are less nervous on an empty stomach."

The council's action follows a Vienna meeting of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which agreed to establish a civilian mission to support democracy and elections, expected in June.
But the 54-nation body, reflecting divisions among its members, did not authorise foreign police or troops, saying the Security Council needed to give the mission a green light.
Seven members of the 15-seat Security Council belong to the OSCE -- France, Britain, Russia and the United States, which are permanent members with veto power, as well as Sweden, Portugal and Poland.

Italy has estimated about 2,500 personnel would be deployed initially, with another 2,500 in reserve. Albania wants foreign police or troops to help secure ports, airports, roads and railroads to ensure distribution of relief supplies.
Whether or not the troops guarding Albanian ports would prevent refugees from leaving is not clear.

Many Albanians have sought asylum in Italy, which on Monday decided to turn away boats heading towards southeast Italian ports across the Adriatic, a journey already made by some 12,000 people since March 13.

Diplomats said the status of the force would be similar to the U.S.-led operation to expel Iraqi troops from Kuwait or France's 1994 intervention. In both cases the United Nations gave the operations international legitimacy without organising the missions.
